title: How to encode a movement that takes two arms
lead: At the National University of Singapore, researchers tested ways to represent two arms' movements in a robot controller. They gave the arms a shared system of codes and used the left arm's plan to help calculate commands for the right.

news.title: Singapore researchers encode one robot arm's movement with the other in mind
news.summary: A National University of Singapore team introduced BiCAT, a way to represent movements of two robot arms with short codes. Across ten simulated tasks it improved mean success by 17.6 percentage points over the strongest of eight comparison methods.
news.details: The model calculates the left arm's commands first. Within each arm's group it predicts the codes in parallel.
news.technical_novelty: BiCAT gives the arms a shared motion representation and uses information from the partner arm to choose codes.
news.engineering_impact: The left arm's plan becomes an input when calculating what the right arm will do.
news.limitations: The gain of 17.6 percentage points applies to ten virtual tasks. Six physical tasks were evaluated separately.
news.evidence_status: The National University of Singapore team published the comparison on November 17.
news.body:
National University of Singapore researchers tested how to encode actions for two robot arms. Their BiCAT method gives the arms a common motion representation and preserves information about their relationship when turning codes back into commands. In simulation, the team measured the difference in task success against eight other methods of encoding actions.

When one arm holds an object, the path the other should follow depends on where the first one holds it. Yet both arms can perform similar movements. The researchers gave them a shared motion representation so that a similar piece of a path can be described with the same system of codes. When choosing the codes for either arm, the model also takes information from its partner into account. A joint decoder, the part that turns those symbols back into movements, reconstructs commands for both arms.

When the controller chooses an action, it first predicts a set of codes for the left arm. It then predicts the set for the right arm using the left arm's prediction. Within each arm's set the codes are predicted in parallel. The joint decoder receives both sets, so at that stage of the calculation it has access to the left arm’s plan and the right arm’s response to it. The researchers compared the methods in the RoboTwin 2.0 simulator and separately evaluated six physical tasks on three robot configurations.

The authors report 40.5 milliseconds to produce a chunk of actions. Reproducing the comparison requires keeping two quantities distinct. The timing applies to a group of commands, while the 17.6 percentage point gain refers to mean success across ten virtual tasks. The paper evaluates its six physical tasks separately.

news.title: A virtual hand's early score proved a poor guide to its next training run
news.summary: Artur Kuramshin and colleagues used simulation to test how to adapt a robot controller to a many-fingered hand. A score taken just after learning from demonstrations gave little guidance about which saved version would make best use of a second training stage.
news.details: In a virtual kitchen the hand pressed a coffee machine button and screwed in a light bulb.
news.technical_novelty: The researchers saved the program at different points while it learned from examples and gave each copy more practice.
news.engineering_impact: That allowed a direct comparison between each program's score after its first lesson and its result after the second.
news.limitations: The tests shifted appliance position along one axis. Contact with the button and the bulb took place in the computer.
news.evidence_status: Artur Kuramshin and colleagues reported the two simulated tests in a paper posted November 18.
news.organization: Mila, Université de Montréal and Renesas Electronics Canada
news.body:
Artur Kuramshin and colleagues compared methods for adapting the π0.5 controller to a simulated many-fingered hand pressing a coffee machine button or screwing in a bulb. They wanted to select a checkpoint, a saved set of parameters from which to start learning with reward feedback. Across the two tasks, high success immediately after training on demonstrations was an unreliable selection criterion.

A person first operated the virtual hand remotely. The researchers used the resulting examples to adapt π0.5, a model that selects movements from visual input and instructions, to the new hand. The original model had not trained on the LEAP hand, which has sixteen degrees of freedom. The team saved intermediate versions as it adapted the model. This let it start the following stage from several points in the same training run, with different amounts of learning from demonstrations already behind each one.

In the second stage, a trainable component selected variations in the movement using feedback about the result. The team tested the controller at the two object placements used in that stage and at two more outside their range. It varied the location of a lamp on the counter in one task and the sideways offset of a coffee machine in the other. All the objects, contacts and finger movements were simulated. The comparison covered five ways of adapting the model and four saved versions for each recipe on each task.

The most steerable version kept the visual and language parameters fixed while fully training the component that selects actions. The comparison hinges on when the measurement was made. The team evaluated starting points before and after steering, and on the button task the relationship between the two scores could even run in the opposite direction.

news.title: Robot arms learn a towel fold from movements recorded away from the robot
news.summary: Brik Meza and colleagues presented HandUMI, a pair of wearable devices that record a person's movements without using a robot. One controller trained on 562 demonstrations completed a towel fold in 12 of 20 attempts on a physical pair of arms.
news.details: A person folded a towel using two tools worn on the hands. The recordings were used to train programs for real robot arms.
news.technical_novelty: Sensors recorded each hand's path and the gap between the parts that gripped the cloth.
news.engineering_impact: People could collect examples away from the robot that would later attempt the fold.
news.limitations: After training on 562 demonstrations, one program completed 12 of 20 folds and the other completed seven of 20.
news.evidence_status: Brik Meza and colleagues described their test on physical robot arms in a paper posted November 17.
news.body:
Brik Meza's team presented HandUMI, a system that records the path and opening of each gripper during a two-handed demonstration without tying the data to the joints of a particular robot. The authors converted the recordings for simulated arms, then ran a separate physical test to see whether controllers trained on the data could fold a towel.

The demonstrator wears a tool on each hand with parallel jaws that slide together and apart. Swappable tips match the shape of the parts that will touch the object on the intended robot. Virtual reality controllers track the hands, while a separate sensor measures the gap between the jaws. This records both the path of a tool and when it closes or opens on the cloth. For another robot, software calculates how its joints would have to move to take its gripper along the recorded path.

The authors tested that calculation on seven simulated arm configurations. A separate physical experiment used a pair of PiPER arms to fold a towel. With the full set of 562 demonstrations, one controller, ACT, completed 12 of 20 attempts. A second, a fine-tuned model called π0.5, completed seven of twenty. Training ACT on only the first 101 demonstrations produced no completed folds in twenty attempts.

Across the simulated transfers, median position error was at most 1.2 millimetres and at most 4.7 percent of episodes were rejected. Those figures characterize the geometric conversion. Whether the machine could actually keep hold of the cloth and complete a fold was assessed by counting finished attempts on the physical arms.

news.title: Cameras on six robot arms help a warehouse stack mixed cases
news.summary: Mujin described six robots working at a new Green Logistics warehouse in Japan. They receive cases from automated storage, locate them and stack them on pallets for shipment.
news.details: At the new Green Logistics centre, six machines receive cases from automated storage.
news.technical_novelty: A camera on the arm measures depth. Software works out where to place the case.
news.engineering_impact: The camera needs no separate stand beside the robot, which helps the equipment fit the available floor space.
news.limitations: Around 500 cases an hour is the rate given for one machine at this site.
news.evidence_status: Mujin, the supplier, described the installation and its rate in a report published on November 19.
news.body:
At the new Green Logistics centre, Mujin placed six palletizing cells at the outlet of an automated warehouse. In a November 19 case report, the supplier describes how it coupled case recognition with the calculation of a stacking position. Mounting vision equipment on the arm freed up space where the cells meet the storage system.

Cases arrive individually from storage. The machines have to stack them on a pallet, a flat base on which several cases can travel together as one load. For an arm, each placement changes the space available for the next case. The MujinOS software chooses a stacking position while the system is working. It uses a view with depth from a camera on the arm to recognize and locate the case in front of it. The supplier says the equipment handles roughly a thousand kinds of cases.

Floor space also shaped the installation. The six work cells sit directly beside the automated storage system, packed into a limited area. Putting the camera on the arm dispenses with a separate stand alongside each robot. The system takes possible collisions into account as it plans the movement. Mujin reports a rate of about five hundred cases picked and stacked per hour for an individual machine at the site.

Reproducing the quoted rate would require a record of the sizes and sequence of the cases arriving during measurement. The supplier identifies the variety of stock and gives an hourly rate per cell, but its announcement does not break down cycle times by case size.

news.title: FamilyMart connects the drinks fridge to the stock shelf
news.summary: Japan's FamilyMart will begin a phased rollout of Telexistence drink-stocking robots in January 2027. Staff load a digital storage shelf, while sales at the individual shop help determine which drinks the robot puts on display first.
news.details: A worker loads the reserve drinks first. The robot moves bottles onto the shelf facing the shoppers.
news.technical_novelty: The system tracks the location of the drinks and uses the shop's sales history.
news.engineering_impact: A drink that sells quickly can get priority when the machine restocks the display.
news.limitations: The roughly 70 percent saving refers to staff time spent restocking drinks per day at the early stores.
news.evidence_status: FamilyMart and Telexistence described the early stores and the phased rollout planned from January 2027.
news.body:
FamilyMart’s drink-restocking system, announced on November 19, uses inventory and sales data to make different decisions about bottles moving through a Japanese convenience store. The shelf records where the stock is, and the store's sales determine which items the machine moves first. The chain plans to deploy the two pieces of equipment together starting in January 2027.

Staff used to handle the same delivery at two points in its journey. They sorted the incoming drinks inside the fridge, then checked what customers had taken and carried bottles from storage to the display. In the new arrangement, the storage shelf marks the handover. A worker scans the first bottle and puts the stock away. The shelf keeps track of product locations and quantities, even when different items share the storage space. It can also suggest how many bottles of each item are needed.

A separate machine takes care of the display. Its control system uses the store's sales history to give popular products priority. The retailer and its technology partner have been working together on the equipment since 2020. FamilyMart quotes a maximum of about 1,800 bottles stocked per day. That figure describes the machine's capacity. To assess the effect on staff, the chain tracked time spent replenishing drinks per store per day.

An engineer evaluating the installation could also measure how long a display slot stays empty during a rush. A daily capacity figure alone cannot answer that question. FamilyMart gave a different measure from the early installations: staff spent about 70 percent less time replenishing drinks.

technology_signal.title: Shared motion codes improved two-arm coordination in tests
technology_signal.summary: National University of Singapore researchers used their prediction for the left arm to calculate movements for the right. Across ten virtual tasks, mean success exceeded the strongest of eight comparison methods by 17.6 percentage points.
technology_signal.implications: In the Singapore team’s BiCAT method, the controller calculates commands for the left arm and passes that plan into the calculation for the right. The researchers evaluated six physical tasks on three robot configurations separately.
